source_history.outcome: Fetch stamps and sequential full-document reading receipts are inherited from the QC planning source ledger; this batch author inspected only the relevant local extracted sections and does not claim to have reread either full document sequentially.

Inspected Cleve §§36.1, 36.3.1, and 37.1–37.1.3 in the cached full PDF text; Preskill §§7.1, 7.4.1–7.4.3, 7.6, 7.8, and 7.15 in the complete PDF; all four MIT Lecture 5 slides; and Axler §7D Theorem 7.49 with its §6A inner-product convention. This records these scoped readings, not a new claim of sequentially rereading the 328-page Cleve or 92-page Preskill documents.

sources.title: Richard Cleve, Quantum Information Processing course notes, QIC 710 / CS 768 / PHYS 767 / CO 681 / AMATH 871 / PMATH 871
sources.locator: §§37.1–37.1.3, printed pp. 292–296 (classical linear codes, Hamming distance, duals, generator/parity-check matrices and syndrome decoding)

contents.name: §37.1, Definition 37.1 (linear code as a linear encoding with a codeword subspace)
contents.support: The source treats binary linear codes; the local definition carries an explicitly stated finite field F and proves its finite-dimensional encoding interface.

contents.name: §37.1, Definitions 37.2–37.3 (Hamming distance and code distance as minimum nonzero weight for a linear code)
contents.support: The binary definitions are generalized to any finite field locally, with the zero-code convention stated separately.

contents.name: §37.1, Theorem 37.1 (distance gives unique decoding below half the minimum distance)
contents.support: The source proves the binary radius claim; the local theorem proves the finite-field claim and separately proves known-erasure uniqueness.

contents.name: §37.1.1, Definition 37.4 (dual of a linear code under the mod-2 bilinear dot product)
contents.support: The local definition states the bilinear dot product over an arbitrary finite field and explicitly avoids a Hermitian inner product.

contents.name: §37.1.2, generator and parity-check matrices, their row/column conventions, and the zero product identity
contents.support: Cleve uses row messages and right multiplication; the local item declares column vectors and proves its n-by-k and (n-k)-by-n shapes.

contents.name: §37.1.2, existence of generator and parity-check matrices for a linear code
contents.support: The existence proof is local and covers k=0 and k=n; Cleve’s source supplies the binary construction context.

contents.name: §37.1.3, syndrome depends on the error rather than the transmitted codeword
§37.1.3, parity-check syndrome table and unique correction for the listed low-weight errors
contents.support: The companion recomputes the syndrome table for the three-bit repetition code; Cleve’s running 7-bit code and row-vector convention are not imported as calculations.

contents.name: §37.1, Theorem 37.1: the distance threshold for unique decoding
contents.support: The source states the bounded-distance decoding threshold; the local proof translates the metric triangle inequality into disjoint closed Hamming balls and handles the zero-code case.

contents.name: §37.1.3, parity-check syndrome of a received word
contents.support: The source defines the parity-check syndrome and analyzes it for received words; the local definition fixes the general finite-field matrix convention.

sources.title: John Preskill, Quantum Computation, Chapter 7: Quantum Error Correction
sources.locator: §7.1, printed pp. 1–3 (quantum code subspaces); §§7.4.1–7.4.3, printed pp. 13–15 (distance, located errors, and error detection); §7.6, printed pp. 18–20 (binary linear codes, matrices, syndromes, distance, and duals); §7.15, printed pp. 50–51 (codes over GF(4))

contents.name: §7.1, a quantum error-correcting code as an encoded subspace of a finite physical register
contents.support: The local interface uses an explicit isometric encoding and proves its projector using the repository first-linear inner-product convention.

contents.name: §7.4.1, distance as the least support weight of a non-scalar code compression
contents.support: Preskill reduces to Pauli errors; this page defines support and distance over all finite-register endomorphisms and proves only detection below distance.

contents.name: §7.4.1, correction of t arbitrary errors from distance at least 2t+1 via the error-correction condition
contents.reason: The QC18 design proves the operator compression detection criterion only; product conditions and construction of recovery maps are assigned to the dedicated QC19 Knill–Laflamme and recovery page.

contents.name: §7.4.2, additional recovery from errors at known locations
contents.reason: This result is a quantum located-error recovery statement, while the present pair proves only classical erasure uniqueness and quantum detection; the quantum recovery hypotheses belong to QC19.

contents.name: §7.4.3, quantum error detection from code-space compression
contents.support: The local theorem proves the compression identity for every operator of weight below the defined distance and explicitly asserts no recovery map.

contents.name: §7.15, quantum codes over GF(4)
contents.reason: GF(4) stabilizer-code representations and their Pauli commutation structure are assigned to later quantum-computing pages; this pair uses finite fields only for classical codes and makes no GF(4) quantum-code claim.

contents.name: §7.4.1, operator weight from tensor-factor support and the distance definition
contents.support: The source defines Pauli weight and extends weight to arbitrary n-qubit operators; the local definition gives the equivalent tensor-factor support interface for finite registers and proves permutation invariance.

contents.name: §7.6, bounded-distance decoding and the distance threshold
contents.support: The source relates minimum distance to correctable error radius; the local proof establishes disjointness directly from the Hamming metric for every finite field.

sources.title: Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed.
sources.locator: §6A, inner-product convention and induced norm (printed pp. 183–186); §7D, Theorem 7.49(a)↔(c), isometry iff inner-product preserving (printed pp. 258–259)

contents.name: §7D, Theorem 7.49(a)↔(c): a linear isometry preserves inner products
contents.support: Axler states and proves the norm-isometry/inner-product-preservation equivalence. The local item supplies an independent four-norm expansion under the root first-linear convention and avoids the broader dependency chain of the root polarization theorem.

canonical.name: The finite-field matrix lemma that a full-column-rank generator has image dimension k
canonical.support: A local prerequisite proved from the matrix entry formula, the finite standard basis, and rank-nullity; neither source is treated as a substitute for this proof.

canonical.name: Dimension n−r of the bilinear dual and the double-dual identity over every finite field
canonical.support: Cleve states the binary dual interface; the local proof establishes the arbitrary-field result using the nonsingular coordinate pairing and rank-nullity.

canonical.name: The Hamming metric proof and equality between code distance and minimum nonzero weight
canonical.support: The metric and zero-code convention are proved locally, including the degenerate zero-code case.

canonical.name: The orthogonal projector associated with a finite-dimensional isometric quantum encoding
canonical.support: The proof derives V*V=I from the locally proved isometry-preserves-pairing lemma and the repository first-linear convention; it no longer imports the root polarization theorem.

canonical.name: Permutation invariance of operator support weight under the declared tensor-factor ordering
canonical.support: The proof follows the actual QC02 position convention and uses inverse wire maps and factorwise tensor maps.

canonical.name: Linearity and encoding invariance of detectability, including existence of the distance minimum
canonical.support: The proof treats all endomorphisms, one-dimensional logical spaces, and finite support subsets locally.

canonical.name: Equal classical syndromes force errors to differ by a codeword and imply equality below half distance
canonical.support: The proof is over arbitrary finite fields and keeps subtraction distinct from addition outside characteristic two.

canonical.name: Zero-code, zero-dimension, and empty-matrix cases in generator/check construction
canonical.support: The local proof explicitly covers k=0 and k=n with n-by-zero and zero-by-n matrices; no choice beyond finite bases is used.

canonical.name: Inner-product preservation by a finite complex linear isometry under the root convention
canonical.support: A local four-norm expansion proves equality of real and imaginary parts. This replaces the root polarization supplier whose published transitive dependencies reach AC through a metric-continuity result.

sources.title: Richard Cleve, Quantum Information Processing course notes, QIC 710 / CS 768 / PHYS 767 / CO 681 / AMATH 871 / PMATH 871
sources.locator: §36.1, printed p. 281 (classical 3-bit repetition code); §36.3.1, printed p. 286 (three-qubit code protecting against one X error); §§37.1–37.1.3, printed pp. 292–296 (binary distance and syndrome method)

contents.name: §36.1, classical 3-bit repetition code and majority correction
contents.support: The source introduces the length-three repetition code and correction of one unknown bit error; the local example computes its parity-check syndromes, erasure completion, and two-error miscorrection.

contents.name: §37.1.3, the one-error syndrome table for the seven-bit running code
contents.support: Cleve’s 7-bit example is a different [7,3,4] code; the local [7,4,3] Hamming matrix and every syndrome are independently verified.

contents.name: §37.1.3, the parity-check method for identifying low-weight errors
contents.support: The local F5 example computes all 16 nonzero one-symbol-error syndromes directly; Cleve’s binary source is used only for the syndrome method.

contents.name: §36.3.1, three-qubit code that protects against one X error
contents.support: The source gives the three-qubit encoded block and syndrome recovery for one X error; the local example computes the projector, X and Z compressions, and the distance-one detection boundary.

sources.locator: §7.1, printed pp. 1–3 (quantum code subspaces and three-qubit bit-flip protection); §7.4.1–7.4.2, printed pp. 13–14 (distance and located errors); §7.6, printed pp. 18–20 (binary linear codes); §7.8, printed pp. 23–24 (the classical [7,4,3] Hamming code)

contents.name: §7.4.2, known-location errors can be distinguished from errors at unknown locations
contents.support: The source discussion is quantum; the companion’s classical erasure-vs-error comparison is established by its own Hamming-distance argument.

contents.name: §7.6, binary linear codes, parity checks, syndromes, and correction of a bounded error set
§7.8, the [7,4,3] classical Hamming code and the parity-check proof of distance three
contents.support: The source’s parity-check columns occur in a different order; the local example verifies its displayed H and G in the repository column-vector convention.

contents.name: §7.1, three-qubit block and one-bit-flip recovery in the Shor-code construction
contents.support: The source describes the three-qubit bit-flip code and its two parity checks; the local example verifies the projector and the detectable/undetectable operators directly.

sources.title: Madhu Sudan, Essential Coding Theory, MIT 6.895, Lecture 5, “Reed-Solomon Codes” (Fall 2004)
sources.locator: Lecture 5, PDF slide 5 (PDF page 2): Reed–Solomon evaluation-code definition and displayed [n,k,n−k+1]q parameters

contents.name: Definition on slide 5: evaluate polynomials of degree less than k at distinct field elements to obtain a Reed–Solomon code
contents.support: The example uses the source definition at points 0,1,2,3 in F5 and proves injectivity, distance, parity checks, and all one-symbol syndromes locally.

contents.name: Slide 5 generic [n,k,n−k+1]q distance claim together with the printed root-count bound
contents.reason: This batch claims only the concrete [4,2,3]5 instance; the slide’s printed root-count bound is one looser than the sharp degree bound needed for its exact generic distance formula, so the local example proves its parameters directly.
